articles.title: Morocco’s pro-Palestine protests challenge Rabat’s deepening Israel ties
articles.summary: Protests across Morocco highlight gap between public opposition to normalisation and Rabat’s closer ties with Israel.
articles.body:
Pro-Palestine protests have spread across several Moroccan cities, with demonstrators demanding an end to diplomatic normalisation with Israel as Rabat deepens ties with Tel Aviv.

The latest mobilisation took place on September 27, at the end of three days of action called by the Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Against Normalisation.

They followed a September 16 announcement that Morocco and Israel would elevate their diplomatic missions to full embassies and appoint ambassadors.

On September 25, the Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes said it had organised 76 events in 45 cities under the slogan “Friday for Al-Aqsa and against normalisation”.

Moroccan media reported gatherings in cities including Rabat, Casablanca, Marrakesh, Tangier, Fez, Agadir, Oujda, Tetouan, Kenitra and Sale. The 76-event figure was the committee’s own count, with no independent national tally of participants.

In Rabat, protesters gathered outside Parliament, while a demonstration in Marrakesh developed into a march through several main streets, according to Lakome. Moroccan media also reported restrictions and arrests in some cities.

The mobilisation faced restrictions in some cities.

In Tangier, local authorities issued a decision banning a planned demonstration on September 27. Achkayen later reported that security forces dispersed hundreds of participants and that more than 12 people were detained, citing its own sources.

Lakome reported that authorities also prevented demonstrations in M’diq, while security forces surrounded a gathering in Agadir to prevent it from becoming a march.

The Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes subsequently condemned what it described as bans, restrictions and arrests.

The response underscored another dimension of the dispute: Opposition to the relationship with Israel has remained visible on the streets, even as the government has continued to develop official ties.

Morocco restored diplomatic relations with Israel in December 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords framework, alongside Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.

On September 16, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz.

The three countries confirmed plans to elevate the Moroccan and Israeli diplomatic missions to full embassies and exchange ambassadors.

Morocco and Israel also agreed to conclude agreements on investment protection and avoiding double taxation, expand direct flights and organise high-level reciprocal visits.

The move therefore goes beyond maintaining diplomatic relations established in 2020. It sets out a broader programme of institutional, economic and transport links between the two countries.

For opponents of the relationship, the embassy agreement represents another step in a policy they have rejected since 2020.

Morocco has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel while continuing to publicly support the Palestinian cause and the establishment of a Palestinian state.

For opponents of normalisation, however, the two positions are incompatible, particularly amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

“What has changed is the political context: Normalisation is being consolidated at a time when the war in Gaza has generated unprecedented public anger and intense images of Palestinian suffering,” Kathya K Berrada, senior programmes manager at the Arab Center for Research, told Al Jazeera.

“What we are seeing in Morocco is a growing disconnect between official diplomacy and public sentiment,” Moroccan activist Mouna Rahiani said, citing the latest Arab Opinion Index, which found that 89 percent of Moroccans surveyed opposed their country recognising Israel, while six percent supported it.

“While the state is moving towards deeper and more formal relations with Israel, Moroccans are still taking to the streets to say that Palestine cannot be treated as separate from our political and moral responsibilities,” she said.

The September agreement has brought an existing tension into sharper focus: public mobilisation against normalisation continues while the state pursues closer institutional ties with Israel.

Berrada said there was an important distinction between official policy and popular opinion, arguing that there is not enough reliable public data to establish how many Moroccans support or oppose normalisation.

The timing also matters for Morocco’s Western Sahara policy. The United Nations Security Council is due to consider the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in October. Its current mandate runs until October 31, 2026.

The September 16 trilateral statement came against the backdrop of US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israel’s support for Morocco’s position on the territory.

For Rabat, the relationship with Israel sits within a wider foreign-policy framework in which ties with Washington and international support for its position on Western Sahara remain important.

For opponents of normalisation, however, that strategic calculation does not resolve their objection to closer ties with Israel, particularly while the Palestinian issue remains highly salient.

Ahmed, a Moroccan sociologist who asked to be identified by one name, said the September 16 move was “a continuation of the trilateral agreement of December 10, 2020”, but that Morocco should make the relationship “comprehensive, not selective or partial”.

The election changes the political backdrop

The protests came days after Morocco held parliamentary elections on September 23.

The final results gave the Authenticity and Modernity Party 97 of the 395 seats, followed by the National Rally of Independents with 66, the Istiqlal Party with 65 and the Party of Justice and Development (PJD) with 54.

The PJD had won 13 seats in 2021. Turnout was 38.08 percent, compared with 50.86 percent in 2021 and 42.27 percent in 2016, according to Morocco’s Ministry of Interior.

It was the PJD in power when Morocco restored relations with Israel in 2020. Then-Prime Minister Saadeddine el-Othmani signed the Morocco-US-Israel joint declaration that December.

The PJD has maintained that opposition to normalisation was a longstanding party position. The party subsequently reaffirmed its rejection of normalisation and relations with Israel, while el-Othmani defended the 2020 decision as a state-level decision.

On September 17, following the announcement of the planned diplomatic upgrade, the PJD’s general secretariat reiterated its opposition to normalisation and to relations and agreements with Israel.

After the election, the PJD’s national council unanimously decided to remain in parliamentary opposition and not participate in the next government.

The PJD’s position has illustrated the limits of using party politics to measure the effect of opposition to normalisation. The party opposed the policy while in government, yet its prime minister signed the 2020 declaration.

Its larger parliamentary presence in 2026 gives the issue a stronger political platform, but does not by itself alter Morocco’s foreign policy.

It has not been established that the Palestine issue or opposition to normalisation was a decisive factor in voting, and neither do the PJD’s gains demonstrate that its position on Israel directly drove its increased representation.

The September demonstrations show that organisations opposed to normalisation retain the ability to mobilise across a wide geographic area. But their effect on government policy is less clear.

“There is an important distinction between state policy and popular opinion. Normalisation is an official state decision, but there is limited reliable public data allowing us to measure the level of popular support for it,” Berrada said.

“It would therefore be difficult to claim that either a majority or a minority of Moroccans endorse the policy.”

That distinction is important when assessing the significance of the protests. Demonstrations can show the strength and persistence of organised opposition, but they do not by themselves establish the views of the wider population or show that government policy will change.

The PJD now has a larger parliamentary presence than it did after the 2021 election, but it remains in opposition. It will be able to voice its opposition to normalisation in Parliament, but will not have a place in government.

At the same time, the September 16 agreement remains part of a broader Moroccan foreign-policy framework involving the United States, Israel and Western Sahara. The Security Council’s consideration of MINURSO in October will provide another diplomatic setting in which Morocco’s position on the territory is under discussion.

For now, the protests demonstrate that opposition to normalisation remains capable of sustained mobilisation, while the government continues to deepen the relationship. Whether that public opposition translates into sustained political pressure remains less clear.

articles.title: US forces are set to exit Iraq after 2 decades, leaving opening for Iran
articles.summary: US forces are set to leave their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, ending a military presence rooted in the 2003 invasion and welcomed by Iran and its
articles.body: US forces are set to leave their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, ending a military presence rooted in the 2003 invasion and welcomed by Iran and its allies as a victory. Iraqi security experts warned the withdrawal could expand Tehran’s influence and help Islamic State regroup.The pullout, agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and implemented by Donald Trump’s administration during its war against Iran, comes after more than two decades of conflict in which 4,500 Americans died.Security analyst Jasim al-Bahadli said the departure removed a longstanding counterweight to Tehran and could allow pro-Iranian militias to gain greater influence over security and political decisions. Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Iran-backed Islamic Resistance in Iraq, called it “a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project”.However, Sunni tribal leader Abdulrahman al-Zobaie said Iraq was not fully ready to assume responsibility for security and warned that the coalition’s departure could create a vacuum.US forces invaded Iraq in 2003, toppled Saddam Hussein, installed a Shi’ite-led govt and fought a prolonged counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011. They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat Islamic State in a war from 2014 to 2017. Around twice as many Americans died in Operation Iraqi Freedom as in Afghanistan, where US forces withdrew abruptly in 2021.Iraq subsequently maintained political and military ties with both Washington and Tehran, while its territory sometimes became a proxy battlefield. A US strike killed Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani at Baghdad Airport in 2020, while Iran’s allies repeatedly attacked US bases.Iran, which seeks the removal of US forces from West Asia, says the withdrawal is a victory for its “axis of resistance”. Washington has accused Iran-backed Iraqi militias of attacking neighbouring countries. articles.title: Florida mom left infant, toddler and 2 other kids home alone while she went on 3-day cruise, officials say
articles.summary: Nathalie Belizaire is accused of four counts of child neglect without great bodily harm.
articles.body: A Florida woman was arrested and accused of leaving her four minor children, including an infant, alone while she went on a weekend cruise, according to police. The suspect, 29-year-old Nathalie Belizaire, of North Miami Beach, is accused of four counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. Belizaire’s attorney denied the allegations. According to North Miami Beach police, the father of one of Belizaire’s children, who is 2 months old, had seen on a post on her WhatsApp story on Thursday “depicting what appeared to be a cruise ticket purchase.” That day, he spoke to Belizaire, who told him she would be dropping the children off with their great-grandmother, police said. But when he went to her apartment Saturday night, he saw the TV on through the blinds and heard the children talking inside, which led him to call 911, an arrest report states. Both police and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue responded and forced entry into the residence. There, “all four minor children were discovered inside ... without adult supervision and were hiding together in the bathroom,” police said. Body camera video showed officers gathering the children and leading them outside. When authorities spoke to the kids’ great-grandmother, she said Belizaire had told her that “she would be dropping the children off because she was going out of town,” but never brought them over. Belizaire’s brother also told police that around 8 p.m. Saturday, his sister texted him, “instructing him to check on her children.” Police said their multiple attempts to contact Belizaire were unsuccessful. An investigation revealed that Belizaire had purchased a three-day ticket to the Bahamas aboard the Carnival Conquest with a sail date of Sept. 25. Belizaire “left all four minor children, including a two-month-old infant and a two-year-old child, inside the residence without adult supervision while the defendant traveled out of town aboard a Carnival Conquest cruise ship,” the arrest report states. On Monday, authorities were waiting as Belizaire disembarked at PortMiami, where she was taken into custody by U.S. Customs and Border Protection and later released to North Miami Beach police. Authorities said she declined to provide a statement and invoked her right to remain silent. “Based on the totality of the circumstances and evidence obtained during the investigation, sufficient probable cause existed to establish that the defendant failed to provide the necessary care and supervision for the four minor children, thereby exposing them to a substantial risk of harm,” the arrest report reads. Belizaire appeared Tuesday in bond court, where her bond was set at $10,000 and she was asked to stay away from the children. “You cannot make this up. It says she went on a cruise and left her children home alone,” Judge Mindy Glazer said during the hearing. “These poor kids, four of them, were home alone for three days. ... I’m just grateful nothing worse happened to these kids.” Belizaire’s attorney said she denies the allegations. “Of course she does,” Glazer replied. “One baby, the baby was born in July of this year. Who leaves a baby alone like that?” Authorities said the children are safe and in foster care.

articles.title: A Russian long-range bomber crashes during training, killing 6 crewmembers
articles.summary: The Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, the Defense Ministry said, adding that one crewmember survived and was hospitalized.
articles.body: MOSCOW — A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, the Defense Ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crewmember survived the crash and was hospitalized with injuries. The statement said that the bomber wasn’t carrying weapons. A team of investigators has flown to the area to determine the cause of the crash, the ministry said. The regional administration said in a statement that the plane crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo on the Zeya River near the border with China. It said the pilots “did all they could to steer the plane away from residential buildings.” The Tu-95 is a nuclear-capable four-engine turboprop strategic bomber that has been in service since the Cold War times. The Russian military has widely used the big warplane to launch conventionally armed cruise missiles at Ukraine throughout the more than 4 1/2-year conflict. Some of the Tu-95s of the Russian air force were destroyed or damaged during Ukraine’s “Spiderweb” operation in June 2025 when it used drones covertly launched from trucks to hit several air bases hosting long-range bombers across Russia.

articles.title: ‘Conspiratorial farce’: North Korea denies planting land mines that injured 3 South Korean soldiers
articles.summary: The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Wednesday rejected South Korean findings that North Korea likely planted the land mines that
articles.body: The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Wednesday rejected South Korean findings that North Korea likely planted the land mines that injured three South Korean soldiers last week, describing Seoul's claims as a "conspiratorial farce."Also Read: North Korean mines likely behind blasts that injured 3 South Korean personnel, Seoul saysKim Yo Jong, a top foreign policy official for Kim Jong Un and possibly the second-most powerful figure in Pyongyang, accused South Korea of making "groundless claims" to create a pretext for "military provocation" against her country.“When a single bullet is hit on our land, they must be prepared for a lot. If the military gangsters fire at our soldiers carrying on the permanent project for the southern border, not warning shots, our border units will take immediate and merciless retaliatory action," the Associated Press quoted Kim Yo Jong as saying. She was referring to the South Korean military as "gangsters."Kim Yo Jong's statement came after South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff on Monday announced a preliminary assessment that the blasts were caused by North Korean mines, following a joint inspection of the site with the US-led United Nations Command.The South Korean military officers were injured in two explosions on September 21 near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the heavily fortified buffer separating North and South Korea.The blasts occurred about 10 metres south of the demarcation line as South Korean troops were clearing a patrol route through a densely vegetated area that had rarely been accessed for decades. The route was being prepared for future inspections with the UN Command after South Korea detected possible terrain changes that could have resulted from North Korean mine-laying.Tensions along the border have increased as North Korea has expanded its frontline fortifications, including mines and anti-tank barriers, and increased the presence of troops near the DMZ. The 248-kilometre-long, four-kilometre-wide zone is among the world’s most heavily fortified borders, with an estimated 2 million land mines buried in and around the area, alongside barbed-wire fences, tank traps and combat forces.The latest incident comes a decade after South Korea blamed North Korea for land mine explosions in August 2015 that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers. The incident triggered a sharp rise in tensions, including military threats, weapons demonstrations and renewed propaganda broadcasts, before negotiations helped ease the crisis. North Korea expressed regret over the injuries but did not clearly acknowledge responsibility.Relations have deteriorated further since early 2024, with North Korea describing South Korea as a permanent enemy and abandoning its previous concept of shared statehood in favour of a hostile two-state relationship. Pyongyang has also rejected US calls to resume diplomacy, saying Washington must first abandon its demand for North Korean denuclearisation as a condition for talks.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank
articles.summary: The resolution cites a ‘lack of accountability’ by Israel’s government and an ‘inability to secure justice’ by the US.
articles.body:
The United States Senate has blocked a resolution that would have required President Donald Trump’s administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.

The resolution failed 47-53 on Tuesday, with senators voting largely along party lines.

It was brought to the floor by Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, and cited a “lack of accountability” from the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an “inability to secure justice” from the US government.

Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the only Democrat to vote against advancing the resolution, while Senator Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, joined Democrats in supporting it.

Van Hollen forced the vote under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which allows individual members of Congress to demand a formal State Department report on the human rights practices of any country that receives US security assistance.

“Violence is raging in the West Bank, & despite the deaths of nine Americans, the wrongful detention of even more, & the daily torment of Palestinians, we have no accountability from the U.S. or Israeli govt”, Van Hollen wrote on X before the resolution was brought to a vote.

The resolution called for an unclassified report within 30 days of adoption. It would have detailed investigations into the deaths of the Americans, the treatment of US citizens held in Israeli prisons, and the conditions facing Palestinian children in Israeli military detention.

The measure cited the deaths of nine American citizens in the occupied West Bank since January 2022, including Shireen Abu Akleh , a Palestinian-American journalist and Al Jazeera correspondent who was shot in the head and killed in May 2022 while reporting in the city of Jenin.

It also included Aysenur Ezgi Eygi , who was shot in the head and killed by an Israeli soldier in September 2024, and Sayfollah Kamel Musallet, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025.

The others were Amer Mohammad Saada Rabee, who was 14; Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohamed Ahmad Alkhdour, both 17; Omar Assad; Khamid Ayyad; Nasrallah Abu Siyam; and Khamis Rabee Jabara.

The resolution also noted the arrests of several Palestinian-American children by Israeli forces.

Among them was Mohammed Ibrahim, a 16-year-old from Florida, who was arrested in February 2025 and held in pretrial detention for nine months without contact with his family. It noted that US embassy officials and lawyers who met him told his family that he had lost nearly a quarter of his body weight, contracted scabies, and was beaten and tortured.

Other Palestinian Americans who remain in custody include Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, 16, and Sama Safi, 20, a student detained in June in raids targeting students at Birzeit University.

The resolution cited rights groups that have documented the deaths of at least 44 Palestinians in Israeli military camps since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Those groups, it said, have documented widespread abuses, including beatings, sexual violence, harassment and threats, “pointing to systemic and deliberate mistreatment”.

It also went on to note a sharp escalation in Israeli settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and stressed that there have been no convictions for the killings of Palestinian civilians by Israeli settlers since 2020.

articles.title: Somali pirates killed five crew members on hijacked tanker, officials say
articles.summary: The deaths appear to be the first at the hands of Somali pirates in more than a decade.
articles.body:
Pirates have killed five crew members on board a Palau-flagged oil tanker off the coast of Somalia before security forces rescued the ship, according to Somali authorities.

The deaths on the tanker, the MT Honour 25, were announced on Tuesday.

They appear to be the first deaths at ⁠the hands of Somali pirates in more than a decade and come amid a resurgence of Somali piracy that experts have attributed in part to the effects of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

The MT Honour 25, which authorities said was carrying 18,500 barrels of oil, was seized by pirates off Somalia on April 21.

The Information Ministry of Puntland, a semiautonomous region of Somalia, said in a statement that a rescue mission had freed the ship and captured 16 suspected pirates.

“Before the operation began, the pirates on board the ship killed five of the crew,” the statement said. “Among those killed were three from Pakistan, one from Myanmar and one from India.”

Four other crew members, three Pakistanis and one Indian, were injured, it said.

In a post on social media, the Puntland Maritime Police Force said the vessel was “safe” and under the government’s control. It said efforts were continuing to find others involved in the hijacking.

The rescue follows another operation last week in which the maritime police freed the Sibu 1, a tanker sanctioned by the US that Somali pirates had hijacked in August.

But 28 of the 41 pirates arrested in that operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, and several Puntland security officials accused local police of complicity.

At least 15 attacks have been reported off Somalia since April, according to officials.

A previous wave of piracy, from 2008 to 2014, disrupted one of the world’s busiest shipping routes, cost the global economy billions of dollars and resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in ransom payments.

articles.title: Inside Silicon Valley’s ‘whisper network’ warning women about 100+ alleged predators
articles.summary: A private spreadsheet containing the names of more than 100 people accused of sexual misconduct is circulating among women in Silicon Valley, according to
articles.body: A private spreadsheet containing the names of more than 100 people accused of sexual misconduct is circulating among women in Silicon Valley, according to a report by the New York Post.The allegations range from drugging and sexual assault to rape. The closely guarded document is being used as an informal warning system for women navigating the tech and venture-capital world, where insiders say reporting misconduct can carry career risks.NY Post, citing multiple Silicon Valley insiders, reported that the list includes prominent investors, businessmen and people connected to major technology and artificial-intelligence companies. One tech worker in her 20s told the paper she discovered the document after speaking about her own experience and was invited to add her account.The existence of the list, however, does not establish the allegations against the people named in it. NY Post itself noted that verifying the authenticity of the accounts was a separate question, while its follow-up report said multiple versions of such lists have circulated in the Bay Area over the years because of concerns about both misconduct and the risk of spreading unverified allegations.Several women interviewed by NY Post said they were reluctant to approach police or publicly identify alleged attackers because of the influence of people in the technology and investment ecosystem.One woman said that she feared that pursuing her case and losing could leave her “blacklisted” by investors across Silicon Valley. Another insider described a culture in which social relationships can overlap with housing, investment, employment and professional introductions, making it harder for people to simply walk away from someone they accuse of misconduct.NY Post reported that several of the incidents described were occurring in so-called “hacker houses”, communal living spaces popular among founders, engineers and aspiring entrepreneurs.Rape allegations at San Francisco ‘hacker house’One of the women who has spoken publicly about the issue is Yehong Zhu, she told NY Post that she reported a former member of the San Francisco hacker house Genesis to police in December 2021, accusing him of rape and assault.Zhu said the man was someone she had considered a friend and that she had repeatedly told him no. She also said people within their social and business circle were reluctant to help her locate him.An attorney for Genesis founder Jeremy Nixon told NY Post that Nixon was unaware of the specific situation Zhu described, but would support law enforcement and prioritise safety.Zhu later posted on X about another woman's experience at The Muse, a San Francisco community house, describing it as part of what she called the darker side of the city's communal-living culture. In the post, she urged people connected to The Muse or considering living there to read and share the survivor's account.The woman whose account Zhu shared described joining The Muse during a three-month trial period while looking for community and stability. In her written account, she alleged that a male resident offered her a ketamine-assisted session in January 2025.She said she made clear while sober that she did not want to have sex. She alleged that the man subsequently gave her several doses of ketamine while remaining sober himself, leaving her heavily impaired, and later had sex with her.The woman said that after she reported what happened to one of the house's founders, her account was described to others as a “grey area” and she was encouraged to participate in a mediated conversation with the man she accused. She also alleged that he was later allowed back into the community while she was still living there.The woman's account also alleges that she was eventually asked to leave the house, while she believed the community was more concerned with preserving its internal relationships than addressing her complaint. She has asked The Muse to publicly acknowledge what happened and explain what steps it would take to prevent similar incidents.NY Post also reported a contrasting account from a former resident of Launch House, another founder community. The woman said she suspected she had been drugged at a gathering and later heard from other women that the same man had allegedly behaved inappropriately toward them.The women later approached the house's founders together, after which the man was removed and the locks were changed. She chose not to go to the police because she could not remember enough of the incident to establish what had happened.A wider problem of reporting and retaliationThe controversy around the private spreadsheet has also brought renewed attention to the informal systems women use when they believe formal channels will not protect them.NY Post reported that 11 additional women came forward after its first story about the Silicon Valley list, with allegations involving sexual assault, retaliation and professional consequences. Tracy DeTomasi, CEO of the now-shuttered nonprofit Callisto, which helped survivors anonymously identify possible links between their attackers, said women needed ways to share information while also holding institutions accountable.Callisto stopped accepting new users in July after about 4,000 survivors had opened accounts, according to the Post. The organisation's closure has added another dimension to concerns about the shrinking infrastructure available to people reporting sexual violence.Private lists can offer women a way to warn one another when they fear retaliation. But they also carry an obvious risk: allegations that have not been independently verified can spread without the safeguards of a police investigation, court proceeding or formal disciplinary process.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump’s policies and
articles.body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US votersThe letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material. ‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulersThe IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. articles.title: Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of workers march nationwide, as police arrest 440 students in clashes at schools.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of civil servants, including teachers, firefighters and healthcare workers, have marched in cities across France to demand higher pay, as students clashed with the police in separate protests over conditions at their schools.

Unions said some 300,000 people took part in the one-day strike action nationwide, while police on Tuesday estimated a turnout of 30,000 in the capital, Paris. The workers also demanded better working conditions and expressed anger at the government’s planned budget cuts .

Protests also took place at more than 400 schools, about 40 of which were blockaded and 44 of which faced attempted blockades.

Ten people, both students and staff members, were wounded, and at least 440 were detained, officials said.

The strikes and the student unrest came two days before the government is to unveil its draft budget and seven months before the presidential election. According to unions, the government proposes freezing base salaries for state employees in 2027 to save 2 billion euros ($2.3bn).

It would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze and the eighth during President Emmanuel Macron’s tenure. Unions say the freezes have cost workers a double-digit share of their purchasing power, and they are demanding a 6 percent raise.

Sophie Binet, general secretary of the General Confederation of Labor, called the protests “a red alert”.

“This anger is not going away. The government must look again at the budget,” she told Al Jazeera. She gave the government 48 hours to reverse the planned cuts before her union decides on further strike action.

The Education Ministry said just more than 11 percent of teachers and other school staff went on strike. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries.

Fewer than 1 in 10 other civil servants took part, and fewer still in hospitals, with the loss of a day’s pay a likely factor in the turnout. France’s civil aviation regulator had warned of flight disruptions at some airports.

Professional firefighters, who say this summer’s huge wildfires exposed a lack of resources, were among those marching.

The government has already unveiled measures to help households cope with a spike in energy prices driven by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, but it has failed to quell the discontent with Macron and his administration.

Students, meanwhile, have been protesting outside hundreds of schools over timetables, class sizes, teacher shortages and overheated classrooms during this year’s heatwaves. The demonstrations began in the Ile-de-France region around Paris and spread to other cities.

In addition to the 10 students and staff members who were hurt, 48 law enforcement officials were injured, authorities said, as students in some places set fire to rubbish bins and hurled projectiles, and officers responded with batons and tear gas.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told BFMTV that 440 people had been detained.

“We don’t have the final tally yet, but I’m told two thirds led to police custody,” he said. “Violence is never legitimate. There is nothing that justifies violence.”

Education Minister Edouard Geffray condemned the clashes on social media.

“This violence is unspeakable,” he wrote, adding that legal proceedings had begun. “To legitimize it or… call for an expansion of the blockades is to endanger both our students and public officials. It is irresponsible.”

In Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income suburb of Paris, Bally Bagayoko, the district’s mayor and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed party, joined hundreds of students protesting at the Lycee Paul-Eluard.

He led them in singing the national anthem and called the protests “completely legitimate”, saying poorer areas received fewer resources than wealthier ones.

Outside the Arago school in Paris, students, some with their faces covered, sat on dumpsters to block the entrance beneath a placard reading “Macron explosion”. A banner at the Helene-Boucher school read “Fewer cops, more money”.

“We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally,” said Mael Breton, a final-year student there. “This is a real problem, especially when there is such a lack of funding… here at our school and in the national education system more broadly.”

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday condemned the high school protests as irresponsible but acknowledged that the “difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed”.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, a hard-left presidential contender, accused the government of steadily dismantling public services as he addressed protesters in Paris and urged his supporters to mobilise against the draft budget.

A Toluna Harris poll on Monday suggested that Melenchon and Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, would advance to next year’s presidential run-off, with Le Pen best placed to win.

articles.title: Britain’s prisons are full. The solution has sparked outrage
articles.summary: For weeks, British media has thrummed with warnings from almost every group connected with the country’s criminal justice system.
articles.body: For weeks, British media has thrummed with warnings from almost every group connected with the country’s criminal justice system. Probation officers are threatening strike action. Victims’ rights groups worry that victims aren’t adequately protected. Prison governors warn of prisons acting as a “revolving door.” Beset by persistent prison overcrowding, the criminal justice system in England and Wales is in the throes of a years-long crisis. And it has been thrust into the spotlight by a controversial measure starting Thursday which will see thousands of prisoners released early, simultaneously underscoring the urgency of the problem and the political minefield constraining any attempts to alleviate it. “You’re running the whole system hot, and that means there is no room for error,” said Pia Sinha, a former prison governor who now leads the Prison Reform Trust, a UK charity. “It’s kind of the equivalent of knowing you don’t have any hospital spaces and you’ve got an epidemic looming,” she told CNN, pointing out that any major event or riots would place near-unbearable pressure on prisons. For newly installed Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the public backlash to the policy represented his first real political test as he sought to balance criticism from grieving families with the realities on the ground. Current government figures estimate that prisons, which hovered somewhere between 97% and 98% capacity last month, will fill up by November without urgent action. The reforms were passed by the UK’s previous prime minister Keir Starmer who aimed to give the system some headroom. As part of this, most of those serving a standard prison sentence will be released earlier than initially planned. Adults convicted of less serious offences will be freed after a third of their sentence (rather than 40% or halfway through); others will be released after serving half of their sentence (instead of two thirds). Prisoners will be released “on license,” equivalent to being on parole, and those convicted of the most serious crimes are excluded from the reforms. “We’ve heard from victims who’ve become very unwell as a result of hearing that news,” said Claire Waxman, the independent Victims’ Commissioner for England and Wales, a government-appointed post which represents victims’ issues and advises ministers. “(They are) not able to work, struggling to live their life.” When Debbie Adlam was informed of the changes, she said she felt “sick.” Her son, PC Andrew Harper, had been married less than a month when he was killed in 2019 while trying to stop a quad bike theft. As he confronted the thieves, he became entangled in a tow strap hanging from their car and was dragged along the ground at speed for more than a mile. Three young men were convicted of manslaughter – one, who was driving the car, received a 16-year prison sentence while the other two received 13 years. Under the new rules, the latter two could have been released within months. “Andrew’s life doesn’t get to come back,” Adlam told Britain’s Telegraph newspaper in July, kickstarting an uproar. Burnham was eventually forced to backtrack on parts of the policy, excluding anyone convicted of manslaughter, death by dangerous driving and historic child sex offenses from early release to appease public anger. Even with Burnham’s changes, however, the probation officers’ union and victims’ rights groups say the system is ill-equipped to cope with an influx of offenders into the community, pointing to years of chronic underfunding and staffing pressures. Longer sentences Prison populations in the England and Wales have doubled over the past 30 years, according to the Institute for Government, a London-based think tank. Sentence lengths have increased in that time, keeping people behind bars for longer and outstripping the number of new prisons being built, even as overall crime rates have fallen during the last decade. At the same time, more people are being recalled to prison for breaching the terms of their parole, and more are held on remand, waiting to go to court. Although the judiciary determines individual sentences, politicians have always been able to influence that process by passing legislation which imposes more punitive penalties – a phenomenon criminologists refer to as “penal populism.” On average, the minimum term for murder cases has risen from 13 years in 2000 to 21 years in 2021, according to the Sentencing Council, the body which issues guidelines on sentencing for England and Wales. For other crimes, the average custodial sentence has risen from 13 months in 2005 to 21 months in 2023. “There is nothing which justifies this doubling of sentence lengths,” wrote five of the most senior former judges in England and Wales in 2024, referring to this trend. And between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power and cut funding to public services following the 2008 financial crisis, just 500 net prison places were created. The Covid-19 pandemic only compounded the issue, creating a backlog for already stretched courts, forcing people to wait in prisons longer before their trial. Further prison building programs are planned but will take years to complete. ‘Instability all through the prison pipelines’ In the meantime, overcrowding “creates instability all through the prison pipelines, and then managing it safely becomes the only show in town,” said Sinha. Staff may have less time to properly assess prisoners, meaning they can be sent to less secure facilities, creating problems for management there. Mistakes are more likely to happen too. Between April 2024 and March 2025, 262 prisoners were released in error in England and Wales – the highest number on record and a 128% increase from the previous year. Meanwhile, prisoners increasingly end up spending more time in their cells, with less access to rehabilitative programs and more incentive to pass the time taking illicit drugs. That, in turn, is helping fuel much higher levels of violence towards prison staff. And with capacity so stretched, it is much harder to upgrade the crumbling Victorian-era prisons which are still an integral part of the prison infrastructure, said Sinha. During her time as governor of HMP Liverpool, in northwest England, between 2017 and 2020 she was able to reduce the number of prisoners there to “rebuild the prison wing by wing,” she recalls. “There is no such capacity now, so that’s the big fundamental difference … In 2017, you would call yourself overcrowded if you were 80% (capacity). It’s now 98%.” ‘How on earth am I going to cope?’ Any attempt to relieve the pressure on prisons shifts onto the probation service, which monitors offenders serving their sentence in the community. But the probation service is “heading for a complete meltdown,” warned Ian Lawrence, general secretary of NAPO, the union which represents probation officers. Their members overwhelmingly voted in favor of potential strike action in August over pay and increasing workloads. “Already without the early release scheme, workloads are at such a crescendo that we’ve never encountered before. Sickness is at all-time high,” Lawrence told CNN, noting that 60% of those off sick are suffering from burnout. “All the mood music among the members is ‘How on earth am I going to cope?’” he said. These crushing workloads create a “more risk averse culture,” Lawrence added, meaning officers are more likely to send offenders released on license back to prison. Although the government announced a £700 million (roughly $925 million) investment into the probation service and plans to recruit thousands more officers as part of its sentencing reforms, Lawrence cautions that those extra officers will need time to understand the complexities of the job. Such dysfunction is already contributing to very high rates of “victim attrition, where a victim reports and then withdraws their support for a prosecution,” says Waxman, the Victims’ Commissioner. It’s a trend she worries this scheme could accelerate, particularly if sentencing isn’t communicated properly. “We’re now hearing from victims saying ‘What is the point? Why am I going to have to wait years to go through the criminal justice system if the end result is that you will release the offender much earlier?’”

articles.title: Nearly 40 kilograms of cocaine held by Fiji court replaced with flour
articles.summary: Nearly 40 kilograms of cocaine stored as evidence for a major drug trial in Fiji were stolen from a courthouse, with most swapped out for flour, local media reported, in a case that highlights the South Pacific tourism hotspot’s struggle against an influx of narcotics.
articles.body: Nearly 40 kilograms (88 pounds) of cocaine stored as evidence for a major drug trial in Fiji were stolen from a courthouse, with most swapped out for flour, local media reported, in a case that highlights the South Pacific tourism hotspot’s struggle against an influx of narcotics. The cocaine, worth 30 million Fijian dollars ($13.3 million), had been seized in a 2019 case involving Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Rahman. He was convicted of unlawful possession, according to official records. The confiscated drugs remained stored at the Suva High Court while appeals were heard – but during an inspection on September 15, officials discovered that seven out of 39 cocaine bars were missing, police said. That kicked off an investigation that ultimately found that all of the remaining cocaine were dupes, and that none of the original seized cocaine remained. “Forensic tests conducted on the remaining drug exhibits have all returned negative,” police said in a statement on Tuesday. “The exhibits were all tampered with and the investigation is focused on those directly charged with the management of the exhibits at the High Court Registry.” Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu said Wednesday that the cocaine was placed in the High Court vault in March 2021, but it’s not clear when the theft happened. The exhibits were confirmed to have been cocaine in a previous test in 2019. Police identified six persons of interest who work in the judiciary department and would have had access to the vault, and one of those people was currently out of the country, Tudravu said during a news conference. Officers were now double checking all other exhibits in the court, including seized cash. The cocaine theft has raised serious questions about security in the country’s judicial system and prompted outrage from the public and lawmakers. “The replacement of the cocaine with flour, whatever it is, that is a sad indictment of … whoever is responsible,” said opposition politician Jone Usamate, speaking in Parliament. “How do you know now that what is in all those exhibits is really what is claimed to be in the exhibits?” Justice Minister Siromi Turaga expressed his “disappointment” and shock, adding that authorities were now working to upgrade security and review existing protocols at the High Court. An archipelago famed for its friendly culture, white-sand beaches and teeming coral reefs, Fiji has struggled for years to contain a drug boom. It has emerged as a crucial transit point for narcotics being trafficked from the Americas to lucrative markets in Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Asia. Massive stockpiles of methamphetamine smuggled onto the islands by cartels have spurred a widespread addiction crisis, seen as a key driver of an HIV epidemic that Fiji recently declared a national emergency. The disappearance of the cocaine “has come at a time when we are talking about transnational crime,” said Turaga, adding that “it goes to show the magnitude of the problem we are facing.” “No one is immune from this. No stone will be unturned. Anyone found guilty will be made accountable,” he said. This isn’t the first such incident, or even the only one this year; earlier in March, police discovered that another 12 kilograms of confiscated cocaine related to a separate criminal case had also gone missing. Local journalists at Wednesday’s news conference pressed the police commissioner on why security hadn’t been stepped up after the March discovery, and whether that could have prevented the second instance of stolen drugs. “All of us are concerned. The government is concerned. I’m concerned about this,” said Tudravu. “That is why we are trying our best to conduct the investigation as fast as we can.”

articles.title: One of Xi’s top security officials has been identified – with the help of a White House guest list
articles.summary: One of China’s most important - and mysterious - security officials has stepped out of the shadows and been identified, thanks in part to a guest list published by the White House.
articles.body: One of China’s most important - and mysterious - security officials has stepped out of the shadows and been identified, thanks in part to a guest list published by the White House. The man, a bespectacled official with a neat crew-cut who has made a handful of appearances alongside Chinese leader Xi Jinping in recent years, has long been considered by China watchers to be Zhou Hongxu, the Director of the Central Guard Bureau, an office similar to the US Secret Service. Beijing has never publicly confirmed Zhou’s job title, and his official biography has few clarifying details. It was only when the White House published a list of Chinese guests and their official titles for the recent state banquet hosted by US President Donald Trump for Xi that Zhou’s official position was finally confirmed. His presence at such a high-stakes diplomatic engagement shines a light on a coterie of younger generation party cadres and security figures that have become some of Xi’s most trusted aides, with the ruling Communist Party’s next national congress that often decides key leadership positions now just a year away. In footage broadcast by state broadcaster Chinese Central Television, Zhou could be seen among guests at the state banquet wearing a buttoned-up Mao suit and standing just behind US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Zhou also made a rare high profile diplomatic appearance earlier this month when Xi he met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. He could be seen sitting between China’s two vice ministers of foreign affairs, according to official footage, although state media did not identify him despite his prominent visibility. Analysts said Zhou’s increased public appearances are noteworthy. “Zhou might be the first ever top security guard being involved in such high-profile diplomatic talk, as far as publicly documented appearances are concerned,” Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN. Deng said Zhou’s appearance at the White House state banquet may suggest “Xi deliberately wanted to bring him into the public eye. “ “And if Xi is intentionally giving him this kind of exposure, it would suggest that he is being entrusted with greater responsibilities and may be given a more important role in the upcoming leadership reshuffle,” said Deng. A mysterious figure at home The Central Guard Bureau is one of the most secretive parts of China’s vast security apparatus. Much like the US Secret Service, it is tasked with protecting China’s top leaders as well as the Zhongnanhai compound in the heart of Beijing where the country’s leadership resides. Chinese state media has described the bureau as “an exceptionally unusual organization, straddling both the police and military spheres, and one that requires the deep trust of the country’s top leadership.” The opacity surrounding Zhou has become common practice as Beijing looks to tighten information about key officials in recent years, especially those who serve Xi directly. China’s state-run Xinhua news agency has reported that he was chosen as one of the delegates to the Communist Party’s 20th National Congress in 2022, a major political gathering that cemented the political authority of Xi by granting him a precedent-breaking third term. He remains a mysterious and low-profile figure domestically, and his past appearances can only be detected from fleeting state media footage when he accompanied Xi to attend major diplomatic gatherings. But there is almost nothing about his education and background – or whether he had a career in China’s military or security services. Older images published by Chinese state media have shown Zhou attending various events with his name card showing on the table. When Xi held a summit with Nepalese President Bidhya Devi Bhandari in Kathmandu in October 2019, Zhou was seen sitting behind China’s leader. Zhou also accompanied Xi to the APEC summit in San Francisco in 2023. Zhou’s predecessor was Wang Shaojun, who died in April 2023. Chinese state media, which only confirmed his death three months after the fact, cited an unspecified illness as the cause. It was only following his death that state media confirmed his position at the time as Director of the Central Guard Bureau. A successor has never been announced. It is likely that, like Wang, Zhou came up through China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA). Zhou was seen attending inspection tour with Wang in 2018 when Xi toured the PLA’s Northern Theater Command and both Wang and Zhou were wearing military uniforms. The Central Guard Bureau was founded in 1950 but it traces its origins back to the period of the Chinese civil war when Mao Zedong’s Communists were locked in battle with their Nationalist foes. Its first chief, Wang Dongxing, was one of Mao personal guards. Wang’s later became the party’s vice chairman and a member of the party’s politburo standing committee. According to a report from state-affiliated media China Net in 2014 – one of the few official articles on the bureau - its organizational structure sits within China’s Ministry of Public Security, where it is known as “Bureau 9”. But it operates independent of the ministry and answers to Xi’s cabinet. Key leadership reshuffle The black box of China’s elite politics has long been a source of fascination for journalists, scholars and foreign governments alike. Speculation and reading the tea leaves within Chinese official announcement and state media reports also tends to intensify in the run-up to major Communist Party meetings. In October next year, the party will hold the 21st National Congress, a twice-a-decade political gathering that usually sees significant leadership reshuffles. Most of current senior officials will be over 70 years old by then, including China’s top diplomat Wang Yi, who turns 73 next year. Observers will watch closely for whether a younger generation of cadres will get promoted into key positions of power, especially the party’s politburo and its standing committee, the equivalent of Xi’s inner circle. Other key younger officials who attended the White House banquet were Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning, 53, Hong Lei, the 57-year-old protocol chief of China’s foreign ministry and Lu Luhua, Xi’s personal secretary, who has become a near permanent fixture for overseas visits.

articles.title: Parents of hospitalized Arizona State hockey player call for coaches to be placed on leave
articles.summary: A lawyer for the family says 21-year-old Matthew Mayich suffered from external heatstroke during a team workout in August and is unlikely to recover.
articles.body: The parents of an Arizona State University hockey player who collapsed during a summer team workout and remains hospitalized are calling for coaches involved to be placed on leave. John and Christina Mayich called on ASU’s president in a letter sent through their lawyer Tuesday to place coaches who ran the Aug. 20 workout, which was led by an Army veteran, on leave “while an independent investigation gets to the truth.” Matthew Mayich, 21, collapsed during the outdoor workout just five days into his start with the team and suffered external heatstroke for which he remains hospitalized and from which he is unlikely to recover, family attorney Rob Carey has said. Seven players, who their lawyer said were not named for fear of retaliation, sent their own letter Monday to ASU President Michael Crow, disputing several findings in ASU’s initial internal report into the incident. Though the letter did not include past instances of retaliation by the coaching staff, the players said they are afraid of being retaliated against because the coaches “decide our playing time, scholarship levels, and roster status.” The Mayiches said Tuesday in their letter: “The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day. And there are plenty of former college and pro players in the Valley who could step in and help.” The university did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. A report it released Sept. 21 accounting for the actions of coaches and staff members that day found an athletic trainer assessed Mayich’s condition, told him to stay down, put iced towels and cool water on him, called 911 and directed student-athletes to help her move him to a shaded area. The seven players criticized the report in their letter to Crow. Timothy J. Casey, their lawyer, emailed the letter and said he verified the identities of those behind it. The players noted that Mayich was new to Arizona, having been in the area for only eight days and having been involved in the hockey program for five. Drafted by the St. Louis Blues, Mayich is from Hamilton, Ontario, according to the NHL. The workout session took place on the morning of Aug. 20, a day when the afternoon high temperature was 104 degrees and the early morning low was 74, according to National Weather Service data. The anonymous players said that the training that morning was different from what is described in the school’s report and that it did not abide by university policy. In its report, the school said temperatures were between 86 and 89 degrees during the workout, with relative humidity between 51% and 46%. The players’ letter alleges the university’s temperature and humidity figures “understate conditions on the field.” They said that the training sessions lasted longer than the university’s report stated and that Mayich got no water during a break that lasted only seconds, because he was one of several players who did not reach the water on time before they were “pushed directly into the next task.” The players added that “extra exercise was used as punishment” and that the workout continued despite some players’ displaying signs of distress. A training plan was not submitted to strength and conditioning coaches, the players said in the letter, and emergency gear, including a tub of water for cooling off, was not present as required. The players allege that the Army veteran leading the exercises left before the final event, saying, “The medicine-ball relays in which Matthew collapsed were run with no one supervising but ASU’s own coaches and athletic trainer.” Head coach Greg Powers is said by the players to have characterized Mayich’s condition after his collapse as “just a little heat stroke” of the type he has seen before, according to their letter. Carey, the family’s lawyer, said by email Tuesday night that Mayich was under the care of the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix. “He is incapacitated with no chance of recovery,” Carey said. Efforts to reach Powers on Tuesday night were unsuccessful. He was asked about Mayich during a video question-and-answer session for news media held by the National Collegiate Hockey Conference last week but refused to answer specific questions about the incident. “Matthew and his family are very much in our thoughts and our prayers and at the forefront of our minds as we try to prepare for a new season,” he said. On Monday, state House Education Committee Chairman Matt Gress and Senate Education Committee Chairman Hildy Angius echoed the players’ claims in calling on Arizona Board of Regents Chairman Doug Goodyear to retain an independent investigator. “We need an independent investigation to determine whether ASU followed its own rules, who was responsible for protecting these athletes, and what happened when Matthew Mayich showed signs of distress,” Gress said in a statement. “ASU should not be left to investigate its own conduct and decide whether anyone should be held accountable.” The incident is being investigated by ASU police. Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell, the top state prosecutor for the region, said Tuesday on X that once ASU police complete their investigation, “my office will review this matter at the highest level.”

articles.title: Morocco’s king appoints the country’s first female prime minister
articles.summary: Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri, of the centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, is expected to build a coalition in the coming days to form a government.
articles.body: CASABLANCA, Morocco — Morocco’s King Mohammed VI on Tuesday named Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country’s prime minister, making the 50-year-old attorney the first woman to hold the position in the Muslim kingdom. Mansouri, who until her nomination also was the mayor of Marrakech, was tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The announcement came four days after results of parliamentary elections were announced, with Mansouri’s centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, the biggest vote-getter. Mansouri, the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden in Tunisia, is expected to build a coalition in the coming days to form a government. Morocco’s electoral system makes it difficult for a single party to win an absolute majority. Her government is expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, while seeking to deliver on promises to fight inflation, raise wages and create jobs. The Moroccan Constitution gives the king, who is the country’s highest authority, the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections. That was a change successfully pushed by Arab Spring protesters in 2011. Before that, the king could name the prime minister without any such restriction. Mansouri joined PAM upon its creation in 2008 by Fouad Ali El Himma, a childhood friend and close adviser to the king. A law graduate from the University of Montpellier in France, Mansouri became one of the party’s top leaders in 2024. She twice served as mayor of Marrakech and was a member of Parliament. Mansouri is the daughter of the “pasha of Marrakech” Abderrahmane El Mansouri, a senior local official who was also Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates. He headed Marrakech’s bar association and was a landowner. Mansouri faced accusations of conflict of interest after a group of unidentified hackers claimed she had used her position for personal gain regarding land transactions in Marrakech. Mansouri denied the allegations, called them defamatory and took legal action. One million of the 15.8 million registered voters in last week’s election voted for the Authenticity and Modernity Party, marking its first win since its creation. The election was the first since the Ceuta migration crisis last July and deadly youth-led protests last year. After the royal nomination, the focus shifts to the coalition that will form the next government. PAM has expressed its willingness to work with all parties, but some, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development Party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have announced they will remain in the opposition.

articles.title: Israel’s Lapid accuses Netanyahu of ‘fear-mongering’ over attack warning
articles.summary: Opposition leader dismisses Netanyahu’s warning of possible attacks during next month’s general election.
articles.body:
Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “fear-mongering” after the incumbent leader warned that the country’s enemies may attack before next month’s general election .

Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party, dismissed the warning after meeting the prime minister on Tuesday.

Earlier in the day, Netanyahu posted an online video that showed him posing in front of a fighter jet at a military base and saying there were “indications that, ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us”.

He did not specify which enemy he had in mind. But in recent weeks, he has issued warnings to Iran, Hamas, Hezbollah and the Palestinian Authority, promising retaliation in the event of an attack.

Lapid requested an urgent security briefing after the warning, and in an online post afterwards, he said he was certain the election would take place on time and that “there is no reason to panic the public”.

“The elections will take place on time, and no one has an excuse to disrupt them,” he said.

He accused Netanyahu of using military bases as “props for election campaign videos” and of failing to heed warnings before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which set off Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. More than 76,000 Palestinians have been killed in the war.

“Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7, and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fear-mongering,” Lapid said. He added: “I of course will not violate the confidentiality of the security briefing but it must be said — security threats must be handled professionally and responsibly.”

The election, scheduled for October 7, is Israel’s first vote since the Hamas-led attacks, which plunged the Middle East into turmoil as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, was first elected prime minister in 1996. In recent weeks, he has had to deny media reports that his partners in the Middle East warned him of a potential Hamas attack, an allegation his political rivals have seized on.

Polls show him in a close race to stay in power.

According to a Reuters polling average, no candidate has a clear path to power. The average shows Yashar, the party of Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has emerged as Netanyahu’s most formidable rival, leading the prime minister’s right-wing Likud party by 2 points.

Based on the average, parties opposed to Netanyahu would hold 64 seats in the 120-member Knesset, 15 more than the parties that back him, but they may be unable to form a coalition.

Lapid is one of several opposition figures in the race. He, Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have agreed to coordinate to remove Netanyahu’s government. Under the agreement announced last week, each leader pledged to work in their constituencies to increase turnout and attract support from various sectors of society to secure a majority and form a new government.

The prime minister said in a separate post on Tuesday that he has held a security briefing with Lapid in which he raised alerts about possible attacks “on the various fronts ahead of the elections”.

He stressed that he holds regular briefings with the opposition leader.

articles.title: Watchdog criticises Norfolk Police's handling before man's death
articles.summary: A force should have flagged mental health services after a family called about their son, IOPC says.
articles.body:
The police watchdog has criticised a force after call handlers told a family raising mental health concerns to ring a locksmith.

On 6 August 2025, Hobie Harrison's parents called Norfolk Police to request a welfare check after he failed to respond to them. He was found dead the next day.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said the force's 101 call handlers should have referred the family to mental health services, but instead suggested they contacted a locksmith.

Norfolk Police said it was reviewing the findings and it had been following the force's Right Care, Right Person (RCRP) policy , which limits officer attendance at welfare calls to cases involving "immediate risk to life".

The IOPC said the call handlers should have asked more probing questions to assess Hobie's level of risk and there should have been a better explanation to his parents about why officers were not sent under its RCRP guidelines.

Hobie's parents, Mark and Roberta Harrison, made a second request for a welfare check for their son to Norfolk Police the following day. Officers attended and found the 30-year-old dead in his flat in Norwich.

In October 2025, the family made a complaint to Norfolk Police over its handling of their call.

In its report, the IOPC criticised Norfolk Police's response to that complaint after the force told the parents officers should not have attended either call, including the second one that led to Hobie's body being found.

The IOPC called that reply "unnecessary and insensitive".

Hobie had previously threatened suicide and Mark said: "We'll never know whether he was still alive when we first called and whether something could have been done.

"He might already have been dead, but we'll never know."

More stories on Right Care, Right Person:

In its findings, the IOPC said it was concerned Norfolk Police may not fully understand the risks of the policy.

David Ford, the watchdog's director of oversight and casework, said: "We have raised our concerns with the force around its interpretation of RCRP and monitoring of the initiative.

"As a result... the force has said it will undertake a review to examine whether there are any organisational learnings."

Norfolk Police said it could not comment further because an inquest has yet to take place, which is due to happen in November.

Hobie had schizophrenia and developmental trauma and was under the care of the Norfolk and Suffolk Foundation Trust Community Mental Health Team. His parents said he had a history of drug use.

The couple adopted Hobie as a child and said he had been in "good spirits" the last time they saw him before his death.

In August 2025, the family said they became concerned he had not spoken to them for more than 24 hours as he usually contacted them "several times a day".

"The non-contact was just... it didn't happen. So, it was very, very unusual," said Roberta.

The couple went to Hobie's flat but could not use their key to get inside because his key was still in the lock on the inside of the door.

"We were 100% certain he was in there and he wasn't responding, so we knew there was something seriously wrong," said Mark.
