Unsure whether they had legal authority to break in, they called Norfolk Police and told call handlers that their son had a history of self-harm and suicidal threats.

After consulting a supervisor, the staff member told them the situation did not meet the threshold for a police response and suggested they consider contacting a locksmith.

"We didn't know how to make a decision at that point or what to do quite frankly," said Roberta.

The following morning, after a second call to police, officers attended the flat and found Hobie's body.

"If the police are no longer going to come, then it has to be very clear who's got the responsibility," Roberta added.

RCRP was first developed by Humberside Police in 2019 and has since been adopted by forces across England and Wales.

The policy is intended to reduce police involvement in welfare and mental health-related incidents so officers can focus on crime and immediate threats to life.

Norfolk Police said the approach, which it introduced in 2024, had reduced officer attendance at welfare-related incidents, from 11,831 in the year before the policy was introduced to 9,229 by its second year.

The force said there was "no defined response" to welfare concerns and the appropriate pathway depended on the circumstances.

The Norfolk and Suffolk Integrated Care Board said support could involve health, social care, ambulance or police services.

A 2024 national agreement on the policy said people experiencing mental health crises should not be left without support.

Some coroners have raised concerns about RCRP. A Prevention of Future Deaths report into the death of Sophie Cotton in County Durham said the policy appeared to overlook that mental health teams could not enter locked premises.

Reports into the deaths of Paul Alexander in West Yorkshire and Andrew Hughes in Manchester also highlighted gaps in RCRP response arrangements.

articles.title: CNN founder Ted Turner bought 113,000 acres in Montana in 1989; decades later, wolves, bears and bison roam the former cattle ranch
articles.summary: South of Bozeman, Montana, a vast stretch of land runs from forested slopes and open meadows to high benches overlooking the surrounding country.
articles.body: South of Bozeman, Montana, a vast stretch of land runs from forested slopes and open meadows to high benches overlooking the surrounding country. The Flying D Ranch, a 113,613-acre property that became closely associated with Ted Turner after he bought it in 1989. Once managed as a cattle ranch, the property was reshaped around bison, native wildlife and the protection of large areas of habitat. Today, mule deer, elk, moose, pronghorn, black bears, mountain lions, wolves and badgers are among the animals found across the ranch. Its rivers and streams also support trout fisheries, while bald and golden eagles are regularly seen over the property.Turner bought Montana’s Flying D in 1989Turner's connection with the Flying D began in 1989, when the media entrepreneur acquired the property south of Bozeman. The ranch covered roughly 113,600 acres and stretched across several distinct landscapes, rather than forming one uniform expanse of Montana countryside, according to Montana Free Press (MTFP). The southern end rises into steeper, forested terrain. Further north, the land opens into rolling meadows before reaching higher bench country. That variation created room for different habitats and helped make the ranch suitable for a broad range of wildlife.For Turner, the property became more than a place to raise animals. It formed part of a much larger approach to land ownership in which working ranches were managed alongside conservation goals.The Flying D became a major home for Turner’s bison herdBison are at the centre of the ranch's identity. Turner maintained a large herd on the Flying D, using the property as a setting for his efforts to restore a species that had once been reduced to a fraction of its former numbers. The ranch was also managed for wildlife rather than being treated simply as a private estate. Its combination of grassland, woodland, streams and higher ground provided habitat for species that require very different conditions.Turner's interest in bison extended beyond the Flying D itself. As reported by MTFP, in July 2017, he hosted visitors attending the International Bison Conference at the ranch, where he examined a bison carcass that had been prepared to show the animal's anatomy.That moment offered a glimpse of the hands-on interest he brought to conservation. Holly Pippel, who moved to Gallatin County from Georgia in 1995 to work as an equine manager for Turner, later recalled spending long periods with him on horseback discussing wildlife, habitat and species under pressure.The Flying D provides habitat for wolves, bears, elk and mountain lionsThe Flying D supports established populations of several large mammals. Rocky Mountain elk move through the property alongside mule deer and white-tailed deer, while Shiras moose occupy suitable habitat in the more wooded parts of the ranch, as reported by Turner Enterprises.Rocky Mountain gray wolves are also among the species recorded there. Black bears, mountain lions, pronghorn antelope and badgers add to the list, giving the property an unusually broad mix of native wildlife.The landscape changes considerably from one end of the ranch to the other, and that matters for animals. Forests provide cover and feeding areas, while open meadows and rolling country offer different conditions for grazing species such as bison, elk and pronghorn.Birdlife is part of the picture too. Golden and bald eagles are seen across the ranch during much of the year, particularly around the open country and waterways.Rivers and streams add another layer of habitatThe Flying D is not defined solely by its terrestrial wildlife. Rivers and streams run through the property, supporting trout fisheries and adding aquatic habitat to the ranch's mixture of forests, grasslands and uplands.Those waterways have also formed part of Turner's wider interest in conservation. Scott Bosse, Northern Rockies Regional Director for American Rivers, said Turner supported work to protect Montana's rivers through his foundation.The ranch itself has continued to function as a working property. Alongside wildlife management and bison production, it has offered hunting opportunities through the Montana Hunting Company, according to Turner Enterprises. That combination of private land management, agriculture, hunting and conservation reflects the way Turner approached many of his Western properties.How Turner used vast private ranches to preserve Montana’s open landscapesThe Flying D was only one piece of Turner's land interests. Over his lifetime, he assembled conservation-oriented properties covering about 2 million acres across the western and midwestern United States. His Montana holdings eventually extended to roughly 130,000 acres across several ranches. The scale made him one of the state's most prominent private landowners and put his approach to conservation under close attention.Turner was also an early supporter of conservation easements, which can protect land from future development while allowing ownership to remain private. That became an important part of his land-preservation legacy in Montana.Conservation became part of Turner's wider philanthropyTurner's environmental work extended well beyond ranches and wildlife. MTFP reported that he directed large amounts of his wealth towards humanitarian and conservation causes, including a $1 billion donation to the United Nations in 1997. The donation was intended to support several areas of international work, including assistance for refugees and children, landmine clearance and efforts to combat disease.His environmental philosophy was also fairly direct. In a 2017 interview with Mountain Outlaw, Turner rejected the idea that economic activity and environmental protection had to be treated as opposing goals. For Turner, land ownership provided a way to put that belief into practice. The Flying D was one of the places where the idea became visible, through bison herds, wildlife habitat and restrictions on future development.The man behind the landTurner's reputation was never limited to conservation. He became a major figure in American media after founding CNN and built interests in sports, sailing and entertainment. At 38, he won the America's Cup, an achievement he later described as one of the high points of his life. He also owned the Atlanta Braves and Atlanta Hawks and became known for a personality that could be as conspicuous as his business ambitions.His private life attracted considerable attention as well. He was married three times, with his final marriage being to actor Jane Fonda. The marriage ended in 2001. Yet people who spent time with Turner in Montana often described a different side of him. Environmental writer Todd Wilkinson, who co-wrote Last Stand: Ted Turner's Quest to Save a Troubled Planet, recalled early-morning walks and conversations with Turner about conservation and the problems facing the natural world.A conservation legacy that remains on the landTurner died on May 6, 2026, at the age of 87 in Lamont, Florida, surrounded by his family. By then, the Flying D had been associated with him for nearly four decades. The property remains a working ranch rather than a conventional wildlife reserve. Bison continue to form part of its operations, while the varied terrain supports the deer, elk, wolves, bears, moose, pronghorn and other species that have made the ranch significant as a wildlife landscape.Its future also sits within the broader legacy Turner left across Montana. Conservation easements on his properties will continue to limit development in protected areas, while the ranches themselves remain privately held landscapes.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
articles.summary: "Backpack" defeated a bear known only as "910" in the final round of the annual competition.
articles.body:
A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing".

Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska.

The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year.

Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months.

His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River.

Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy".

But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty".

"I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote."

The finalists' latest weights have not yet been revealed. But adult male brown bears average up to 408kg in mid-summer and often pack on the equivalent of 25% of their body weight by autumn. The largest males can weigh more than 540kg .

Females are smaller but can reach weights of over 300kg. Cubs are born weighing roughly half a kilogram.

"During hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Their winter survival depends on accumulating ample fat reserves before entering the den," organisers wrote.

From June until mid October, the bears gorge on food, including salmon caught with their jaws or paws.

Backpack's biography says his "quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River".

Last year, over 1.7 million votes were cast from more than 100 countries to crown the competition's heavyweight champion.

articles.title: ₹4.26 crore spent on ‘new’ check dams at existing sites, CAG flags possible fraud
articles.summary: CAG flags possible fraud in Odisha as ₹4.26 crore spent on seven “new” check dams built at sites where dams already existed under MATY scheme.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has flagged the possibility of fraudulent payments in Odisha’s water resources department after finding that Rs 4.26 crore was spent on constructing seven check dams at locations where such structures already existed.In its compliance audit report for the year ended March 2024, tabled in Odisha Assembly on Monday, CAG said it examined geo-tagged data and satellite imagery of check dams taken up under the Mukhyamantri Adibandha Tiari Yojana (MATY). The audit found that despite geo-tagging of existing structures, fresh agreements were executed and public funds released for the construction of new check dams at the same sites.The audit scrutinised 331 of 481 check dams constructed in 12 sampled minor irrigation divisions and cross-verified their locations using Google Earth Pro and geo-tag credentials provided by the divisions. It found that seven check dams in four divisions were already in existence when fresh construction contracts were awarded. Yet, expenditure of Rs 4.26 crore was incurred between April 2023 and January 2025 for their construction.“Incurring expenditure on construction of check dams that may have already been in existence indicates a possibility of fraudulent payments which needs to be investigated by appropriate authorities,” the audit report observed.The check dams were taken up under MATY, a state scheme aimed at improving irrigation facilities and recharging groundwater through the construction of check dams. The water resources department had also directed geo-tagging of check dams in 2022 to help identify existing structures and prevent duplication. However, the audit found that despite geo-tagging, fresh agreements were executed for structures that were already present.Responding to the audit observation, govt stated that some of the structures identified by audit had been constructed earlier and were visible in Google images before the new agreements were executed. In one case, it contended that the structure seen in satellite images was an earthen bund built by local people. Govt also disputed one of the locations identified by audit.CAG, however, rejected the explanation, noting that the concerned superintending engineers had executed fresh agreements and made payments of Rs 4.26 crore for construction of new check dams at those locations. articles.title: Family's love of books helped Wellington author break stereotypes
articles.summary: Nadia Shireen says people from South Asian backgrounds were not expected to become authors.
articles.body:
An author who said she defied expectations to write children's books believes her family's love of reading helped her fulfil her dream.

Nadia Shireen from Wellington in Shropshire has had a series of picture books published by Penguin, but recalls growing up at a time when people from South Asian backgrounds were rarely seen as writers.

She said: "I was growing up in the 80's and authors were not people who like me or like my mum or dad."

"If you were South Asian, you obviously encouraged to get a good education and get a steady become a doctor, a lawyer, accountant, or any of those things," she added.

What made the difference, she believes, was being encouraged to read from a young age.

She said: "I was lucky enough to grow up in a house of readers.

"Every week my mum would take me to Wellington library and she would go off and get Agatha Christies and I would go off into the children's book area and I would have a whale of a time just kind of going through all the books."

"It was just woven into everyday life," she said.

Shireen said she enjoyed making her own magazines and comics when she was a child, but ended up studying law at university and then went to work for a magazine publisher for 10 years.

Although it was not books, she admitted it was "still a pretty interesting media career".

Drawing was still a passion though, and she said: "If you've got that creative energy in you, you'll find that you can't really keep a lid on it even if you try really hard."

"I just kept doodling like I've always done," she added.

"I just couldn't stop doodling and drawing."

In 2007 she was accepted onto an MA course in Children's Book Illustration at Anglia Ruskin University, Cambridge as a mature student.

The picture book she produced for her graduation show got the attention of publishers, which she said was a "dream come true".

Her debut book Good Little Wolf received a mention in the Bologna Ragazzi Opera Prima Award and won the UKLA Book Award.

She has since been shortlisted for the Roald Dahl Funny Prize and the Waterstones Children's Book Prize and said: "I could never in a million years imagine that this is what I'd be doing."

Children not encouraged to follow dreams

Shireen's first book was published when she was in her 30's and looking back, more than a decade later, she said she felt incredibly lucky.

"I get to sit at home, write funny stories about animals, draw the pictures, and then, you know, go see my name on the cover of books and get to meet my readers, which I absolutely love," she said.

She also said she got a "real buzz" out of seeing the drawings made by children today.

But she said it had been very different when she was young, and children like her had not been "encouraged to follow their creative dreams".

She said: "I'm not trying to blame anyone, but it's just not something we saw, was it?

"We didn't see brown faces being people who wrote."
